label: JZ Mock C · Paper 2 · Question 1
knowledgePattern: Distinguish a forced divisor from a failed converse and an existence claim
solution:
Since 12=22·3, divisibility of n2 by 12 forces n to contain a factor 2 and a factor 3. Hence n is divisible by 6, proving I.

For n = 6, its square is 36, divisible by 12, but n itself is not divisible by 12. This refutes II and supplies the witness required by III. Therefore I and III are true. Answer F.

hints.title: Factor 12 first
hints.body: Write 12 as a product of primes. When n is squared, what happens to the number of copies of each prime?
hints.recap: Squaring doubles the exponent of each prime factor.
hints.pitfall: A square may contain more copies of a prime than the original number.
hints.pause: Work out which primes must divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, then check statement I.

recall.reminder: Test divisibility by comparing the exponents in the prime factorisations.

hints.title: Try the smallest allowed values
hints.body: List a few positive integers whose squares are multiples of 12. For each, check whether the number itself is a multiple of 12.
hints.recap: One allowed example can disprove an always-claim or prove a there-exists claim.
hints.pitfall: Many successful examples do not prove that a statement is always true.
hints.pause: Use your list to decide II and III. Give a reason for each, then choose the option.
